text: I am comparing Q’s continuous double auction and P’s enforceable, self-negotiated contracts. Initial candidate: distinguish failed price discovery from failed credible commitment by adding a contract layer to Q, but I will check whether Q’s spot settlement already removes the hold-up mechanism that drives P before treating this as a research direction.

I am testing whether P\x27s enforceable, self-negotiated contracts can diagnose or repair Q\x27s slow double-auction convergence, with particular attention to whether Q\x27s instantaneous exchange leaves any commitment problem for a contract to solve. I will check mechanisms and results before proposing a claim.

Direct transfer limit: Q, Trading Mechanism and Information and Objective (lines 239-278), executes a crossed quote immediately and defines per-trade profit \(v_i-p_t\) or \(p_t-v_i\); no later bilateral performance is required. P, Pay for Partner and Contracts (lines 196-204, 248-303), studies promises of future tile coverage and enforces them with programmatic tile/points contracts. Therefore P’s hold-up cure cannot explain Q’s baseline undertrading. Q instead attributes low volume to repeated \(\$0.01\) quote improvements and failure to cross before its 300-iteration cap (lines 351-381). I am testing a different connection: reference/commitment representations may anchor agents and suppress feasible execution in both settings.

Mechanism mismatch, with a narrower opportunity: Q Method/Trading Mechanism (lines 239-258) makes any crossing bid or ask execute immediately at the standing quote, while Q Results/Individual Behavior (lines 359-374) attributes low trade volume to penny increments and refusal to cross. P Contracts (lines 248-302) target delayed Pay-for-Partner defection via automatic future transfers and penalties. Thus simply adding P-style enforcement to Q cannot directly cure a broken promise: Q already has firm executable offers. I am sharpening the question to whether redundant contract representation changes LLM trading behavior, especially anchoring, rather than assuming contracts add a missing commitment technology.

Candidate publishable test: representational redundancy in a firm-offer market. Formal boundary: for one buyer with value \(v\), one seller with cost \(c\), immediate trade at \(p\) gives \((v-p,p-c)\). A budget-balanced transfer \(t\) from buyer to seller, contingent only on that same trade, gives \((v-p-t,p+t-c)\), exactly trade at \(p+t\); it adds no payoff or allocation possibility. Q already has binding, immediate crossable quotes (Method, lines 239-258), so P\x27s PTC/PPC-style enforcement cannot mechanically solve Q\x27s missing-trade problem under those assumptions. Yet P reports natural-language contracts reduce further trading despite similar covered moves (Results, lines 415-423; Appendix regular-trading lines 1379-1403), and Q reports opening-offer anchoring (Individual Behavior, lines 383-407). Hypothesis to test, not finding: redundant natural-language commitment summaries of an unchanged order book may intensify anchoring and reduce spread crossing/efficiency relative to matched structured summaries. Randomize representation while holding market rules, executable offers, information, and horizon fixed; log initial opposing quotes, crossing hazard, trade count, efficiency, price dispersion. A null result is informative. Limits: P\x27s two-player sequential dependency differs from Q\x27s 22-agent immediate exchange; P\x27s observations are not causal evidence in Q.

Alternative to the redundant-contract hypothesis: compare aggregate efficiency with voluntary individual gains. Q Method footnote (lines 211-215) explicitly permits offers that yield negative profits; Q’s allocative efficiency sums buyer and seller profits (lines 295-301), so its headline welfare does not certify each trader’s reservation-price constraint. P Metrics (lines 238-244) introduces an outside-option test \(BBB=\mathbf{1}\{r_i>b_i\ \forall i\}\), and P Results (lines 418-419) finds that programmatic tile contracts raise the dependent player’s reward on asymmetric boards by 68% while the independent player gets no significant gain, leaving mutual benefit elusive. Joint question: when do LLM institutions raise aggregate gains but fail voluntary participation? A common evaluation would report joint surplus together with each agent’s payoff against its outside option, and experimentally compare contract or market interventions on this constrained frontier. This is an evaluation proposal, not yet an empirical finding about Q’s loss rate.

Cross-check of emmy #6: Q indeed says the mechanism does not constrain offers to nonnegative profit (Market Environment footnote, lines 211-216), and its efficiency is aggregate surplus (Results, lines 296-301), so the welfare metric can mask a loser. Example: \(v=2.25\), \(c=1.75\), \(p=2.50\) yields buyer \(-0.25\), seller \(0.75\), aggregate \(0.50\). However this is a logical possibility, not observed Q loss incidence; we need transaction-level data before claiming actual harm. Also P\x27s \(BBB\) uses strict \(r_i>b_i\) (Metrics, lines 238-244), so \(BBB=0\) can include weakly individually rational outcomes where an independent player merely matches baseline. For Q, report negative-profit rate and \(\pi_i\geq 0\), with a separate strict-gain statistic; do not read P\x27s zero BBB as proof of violations.

Sharper cross-paper identification issue: Q, Market Environment (lines 211-237), deliberately uses symmetric supply/demand; Individual Behavior, Opening-Offer Anchoring (lines 386-403), reports that the second side anchors on the first offer despite no exchange rule forcing it. P, Board Types (lines 212-219), always makes P-Red the independent player on asymmetric boards; Appendix First Mover Advantage (lines 984-993) says P-Red initiates every contract and gets about 60% of negotiated points even on Independent and Mutually Dependent boards. Thus P’s observed red advantage in asymmetric point contracts mixes outside-option power with proposal order (and possibly color/role); P itself suggests a first-mover effect but cannot identify its size because initiator is fixed. A concrete experiment is a within-board factorial: mirror chip colors to switch which role has the outside option, independently randomize first proposer, and hold model pairing and contract terms format fixed. Measure opening demand, final net point transfer, both agents’ payoff against outside option, and joint reward. Interaction tests whether outside-option power amplifies anchoring. This would extend Q’s anchor diagnostic to binding contract bargaining and sharpen P’s power claim; current papers do not establish causal effect sizes.

Correction to my #7 and emmy #6: Q\x27s mechanism permits loss-making offers, but its actual prompts explicitly say \x22Under no condition\x22 buy above or sell below reservation, and announcement prompts repeat those bounds (Q Appendix Prompt Templates, lines 548-578). If every agent obeys them, every trade is weakly individually rational: a buyer who rests has \(b\leq v\), a seller who rests has \(a\geq c\), and a crossing agent also respects its bound, so the resting price lies between \(c\) and \(v\). Negative profit is therefore a prompt-compliance failure, not a generic gap in the reported efficient outcomes. Q does not give its incidence in the paper. This narrows the participation-line novelty substantially; auditing violations could still matter.

Prior-work search (no novelty inference): queried \x22site:arxiv.org large language model continuous double auction contract framing anchoring trade volume\x22, \x22site:arxiv.org LLM agent markets binding commitments contracts double auction price convergence\x22, and \x22site:arxiv.org natural language contracts anchoring LLM agents trade volume\x22. Adjacent studies surfaced: bilateral trade with binding offers vs natural-language messages, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16472; natural-language contracting in sequential supplier tasks, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10475; supply-chain bargaining/patience, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07538. These make a generic \x22language and contracts affect trade\x22 claim weak; a representation-controlled, already-enforced CDA test is the distinct question I can support from Q and P.

Ada #9 is right and narrows my #6: although Q’s exchange does not mechanically reject loss-making quotes, its system/user/announcement prompts explicitly bound bids by buyer reservation and asks by seller reservation (Q Appendix lines 518-527, 564-579). Thus negative realized profit would require agent noncompliance; Q does not report it. My strongest independent line is #8, separating proposal-order anchoring from true outside-option bargaining power in P. Exact Q passage is Opening-Offer Anchoring, lines 397-402. P already notes possible first-mover advantage (Appendix lines 984-993), so the advance would be a causal factorial, not a claim that P overlooked the pattern.

Prior-work check for #8 (no novelty claim): searched "site:arxiv.org LLM negotiation first mover advantage anchoring opening offer bargaining power experiments", "site:arxiv.org colored trails language model first mover outside option bargaining contracts", "site:aclanthology.org LLM negotiation first offer anchoring bargaining", and narrower outside-option/first-mover queries. Relevant studies already report LLM anchoring in price negotiation (Takenami et al., https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.240/) and initial-offer anchoring plus strategic dominance in multi-turn bargaining (Ríos et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09254). Thus generic anchoring is not new. The candidate contribution is identifying proposal-order, role, and outside-option effects separately in enforceable resource/point contracts, where P has them partly bundled. Search did not establish that this exact design is absent elsewhere.

My best cross-pair line, sharpened from \x22can contracts repair Q?\x22 to \x22does contract-like language change trading when execution is already guaranteed?\x22. Q Trading Mechanism (lines 239-258) says crossing executes immediately; GPT Large nonetheless posts penny improvements and reaches only 2.2-3.8 trades per round with efficiency 0.36-0.67 (Results, lines 359-361), and Q reports opening-offer anchoring (lines 386-404). P PTC enforces delayed chip coverage, improving mean normalized joint reward from 0.77 to 0.89 (Results, lines 406-415), but P NLTC has similar contract-covered moves and fewer subsequent arrangements/accepted trades, with agents more often citing the contract as a reason not to trade (lines 418-423; regular trading appendix lines 1379-1403). Test in Q\x27s CDA: hold binding book, reservation schedules, valuations, information, horizon and numeric quote history fixed; randomly show identical resting offers as terse structured records, concise natural-language commitments, or neutral length-matched prose. Give agents unchanged numeric action interface. In paired market seeds, measure opponent\x27s first quote response to randomized but identical initial price across display arms, probability/hazard of crossing a profitable spread, trades by deadline, allocative efficiency, and price dispersion. Compare the representation effect on identical decision states before using full dynamic market outcomes; include prompt-length control and model/role strata. The market should show an effect even with no possibility of defection if cognitive framing is the channel; a null would limit transfer of P\x27s anchoring finding. Distinguish this from P\x27s original commitment gain; its settings have sequential dependence and two agents, while Q has instant exchange and 22 agents. The payoff equivalence in #5 assumes a single homogeneous unit, quasi-linear utility, transfer contingent only on that same trade, feasible effective prices, no third parties, no delayed state contingent terms. It does not rule out effects of richer future obligations or altered strategy. I have no experimental result for the cross-pair hypothesis.

Formatting correction to #13: the literal x22 escape markers there mean quotation marks. The sharpened question is: Does contract-like language change trading when execution is already guaranteed? The study is a causal proposal, not an observed effect. I also find emmy #8 sound as a separate identification study: P itself acknowledges an apparent first-mover advantage but fixes P-Red as proposer and as the strong party on asymmetric boards; randomizing proposer and strong role would separate those effects. My own line pursues representation in an already binding market, which that study does not address.

Preferred publication question (sharpened from “do contracts help Q?”): How much apparent bargaining power in LLM-written, enforceable contracts comes from a real outside option, and how much from moving first? Q’s symmetric double auction shows the first quote anchors the opposite side even without a mechanical obligation (Q lines 211-237, 397-402). P fixes the independent asymmetric player as P-Red (P lines 212-219), fixes P-Red as first contract proposer, and reports roughly 60% of negotiated points to Red even on non-asymmetric boards (P lines 984-993); P also finds P-Red’s asymmetric contract terms improve with full state visibility (P lines 684-690). Run P’s programmatic points contract on paired original and red/blue color-swapped boards; independently randomize which player proposes first, preserving model pair, board geometry, budget, negotiation limit, and judge. The color swap preserves the game’s feasible outcomes while reversing which named player has the outside option. Compare net point transfer and final reward to the independent player across the four role/order cells, plus agreement rate, joint reward, and each player’s gain relative to baseline. A persistent independent-player premium when that player moves second supports genuine power; a large proposer premium on symmetric boards and reversal when the weak player starts supports order effects; an interaction measures amplification. Record first numerical proposal and concession path; these are diagnostics, not causal proof of cognitive anchoring. For anchoring itself, add a separate randomized, explicitly nonbinding numerical reference. Main limits: Q and P only provide observational patterns; P already notes first-mover advantage; existing anchoring studies mean novelty requires this crossed identification and payoff consequences, not a generic “LLMs anchor” claim.
